learn.title: Not just numbers
learn.body: Searching works on any data, but you must be able to ask whether two items match. For int that is `==`. Strings and structs need more care.

learn.title: Comparing strings
learn.body: A C string is an array of characters, so `==` would only compare addresses, not letters. To compare contents use `strcmp` from string.h. It returns 0 when two strings are equal. Never use `==` to compare strings.

learn.title: Searching an array of names
learn.body: The loop is the same as before. Only the comparison changes.

learn.title: Searching structs
learn.body: Each item holds a name and a number. We compare the name and return the number.

learn.title: Looking up Bo
steps: `i` is 0: `strcmp` of Ada and Bo is not 0
`i` is 1: `strcmp` of Bo and Bo is 0

learn.title: Search by a key
learn.body: For structs you pick one field as the key, here the name. Searching finds the struct whose key matches, and you then use any field you like. The shape of the algorithm does not change.
Sorted strings can be binary searched too. Compare with `strcmp` and use its result: below 0 means the first string sorts before the second.

questions.prompt: Which function compares the contents of two C strings?
questions.explanation: `strcmp` returns 0 for equal strings. `==` only compares addresses.

questions.prompt: `strcmp(a, b)` returns \_\_ when the strings are equal.
questions.explanation: A result of 0 means equal. Non-zero means they differ.
"Ed" is not there, so the loop finishes and returns -1.

questions.prompt: Why is `names[i] == t` a poor way to compare strings?
choices: It only works for short strings
questions.explanation: Two equal strings in different places have different addresses, so `==` may say they differ.
